extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, humorists, literary critics, and students of comedy and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical guidance on how to observe, design, and stage comic characters and comic effects—what makes something laughable, the social function of laughter, and specific comic types (e.g., professional comic, Don Quixote type). Useful for writers, dramatists, and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic imagination vs. comic observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic imagination composes characters from inward observation (the poet reproduces life by plumbing his own nature); comedy's observation is altogether different—directed outwards and concerned with others rather than the author's inner self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to create comic characters by inwardly patching fragments of personality; instead observe others externally. Comic observation will be more general and surface-level than poetic character-creation; the comic artist must prefer outward, comparative observation (examples: contrast between poetic character-creation and comedic types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation should be external and general
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic observation is always external and the result is general—it deals with persons at the point where they resemble one another and abstracts/ generalises like the inductive sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic material, seek observable, repeatable traits (skin-deep points of contact between people) rather than deep, idiosyncratic psychological causes. Treat comic features as categories drawn from comparison of analogous cases (method akin to physicist grouping facts under laws). Avoid penetrating too far into individuality or deep causes, which removes the laughable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise causes in an intermediate region of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: For something to invite laughter, its cause must appear localized in an intermediate (not deep) region of the personality—something observable from without and capable of being corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the source of the comic recognizably superficial and correctable (a removable parasite-like mental attribute). If causes seem too deep-seated, the humorous effect is endangered or lost; the comic should appear as an average effect accessible to social correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal comic character: deep-rooted yet superficial (list of desiderata)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideally comic type must be deep-rooted (to supply inexhaustible matter) and yet superficial (so it remains within comedy); invisible to its owner but visible to everyone else; extremely considerate to itself and troublesome to others; immediately repressible yet apt to reappear; inseparable from social life though insufferable to society; capable of being attached to many vices and even to some virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist of opposing features when designing comic types—these tensions (deep yet superficial; unconscious to self but obvious to others; socially pervasive yet reproachable) generate ongoing, varied comic situations. The original wording enumerates many elements to be fused; these can be treated as independent knobs to adjust for variety and longevity of comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as the central comic element
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity is described as the readily available mixture that supplies comedy: widespread, both superficial and deep-rooted, not quite a vice but drawing other vices into its orbit; the one failing that is essentially laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vanity as a seed comic fault: its minor wounds, unreal services, and persistent gratitude make it rich material. Laughter functions as the specific remedy for vanity—play up the self-admiration that becomes automatic and socially problematic to provoke corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effects can arise from low and high elements (transferability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any simple laughable image can worm into images of more complex nature (high comic from low), and conversely many coarse effects result from a drop from a subtle comic element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage simple, concrete images (a short man bowing under a door, the frog-and-ox analogy) as building blocks for more elaborate comic scenes; likewise, trace grander comic sources (e.g., vanity) to explain apparently coarse effects. Avoid assuming coarse effects lack subtle origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential condition: peculiarity must appear as a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A peculiarity observed should straightway appear as a kind of category into which a number of individuals can step—comedy abstracts individuals into types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When spotting a comic trait, present it so it feels replicable (a type, trade, or social category), not merely an isolated oddity. The process of abstraction/generalisation is central: sketch traits that suggest many persons might exhibit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional comic (readymade categories from trades/professions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's divisions of labour (trades, public services, professions) create ready-made categories whose corporate members share habits and peculiarities—forming small societies that provide comic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit occupational stereotypes and shared professional habits as comic types (these are predictable, recyclable sources of comic material). Be aware that such groups arise from social organization, and laughter's business is to repress separatist tendencies by converting rigidity into plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional vanity and solemnity
rubrics_metrics.description: Each professional group may display professional vanity (exalting its own art above others); the more questionable the profession, the more its practitioners may assume a priesthood and solemnity, producing comic effects (example: Molière's doctors treating nature as appendage to medicine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create comic figures, intensify professional self-importance and solemn rhetoric; dubious or quack professions are particularly fertile. Use exaggeration of claimed priesthood and self-importance to reveal absurdity and provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional callousness (rigidity of function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters tightly jammed into the frame of their functions lack room to move or be moved like other people, producing comic callousness (example: Perrin Dandin’s 'Bah! it always helps to while away an hour or two').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray professionals whose duties have hardened them into indifference or routine responses to human situations; the oblivious, ‘that’s the job’ attitude can be used for darkly comic moments. Keep tone consistent with coarse comic effect or refine it with added peculiarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional jargon applied to everyday affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Confining a profession within its own jargon—applying technical language to ordinary life—creates ludicrous effects. This tends to be coarse unless combined with other character peculiarities (examples: Régnard's gambler-speech, Molière's learned women translating science into feminine sensibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place domain-specific terms into trivial exchanges to highlight absurdity; to refine, mix jargon use with eccentric personality traits so the joke relies on both context and character rather than mere vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional logic (particular vs universal reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ways of reasoning customary in particular professional circles are valid within those circles but appear untrue or absurd to the general public; the contrast produces specific comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes where a character applies internal, profession-specific logic to general situations, exposing the mismatch. Explore this as a rich source of comic misunderstanding and critique of insularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic logic: inversion of common sense (Don Quixote type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic absurdity often consists in moulding things to an idea instead of moulding ideas to things—seeing what one thinks rather than thinking of what one sees (Don Quixote sees giants where others see windmills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters dominated by a privileged recollection or idea that orders perception; let them interpret neutral stimuli to fit their obsession and then develop the illusion logically in its consequences. This yields a comic absurdity that is special, not generic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism, rigidity and obstinacy produce comic error
rubrics_metrics.description: At the root of the comic there is rigidity—automatism or obstinacy of mind or disposition—forcing characters to pursue one path, continually recur to one idea despite interruptions, and to see only what they want to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray stubborn single-mindedness (repetition of an idea or action) to generate predictable but escalating comic effects. Many Molière scenes exemplify this: the character’s refusal to adapt is itself the comic engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation of rules of reasoning (dream-like thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable often involves a relaxation of strict reasoning: false reasonings that resemble dream thought, abridged arguments (witticisms) that give only beginning and end, or play upon word-sound over meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truncated or superficially logical chains that mimic dozing thought—sufficient structure to be plausible but lax enough to mislead. Devices: non sequiturs that feel internally coherent, wordplay where sound overrides meaning, staged whisper-repetition that collapses into nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and crescendo toward absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of images or phrases and a gradual progression (crescendo) of concessions toward absurdity produce a distinct comic sensation (seen in dream logic and plays like Monsieur de Pourceaugnac or Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure comic sequences so that small concessions accumulate into larger absurdities; use recurring motifs or refrains to build expectation and then subvert it. The crowding of absurdities can simulate dream drift and yield strong laughter when released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion/confusion of identities (dream-like mixture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams often fuse two persons into one who is both self and other; similar confusions in dialogue or narrative produce a unique comic absurdity (example: Mark Twain’s twin dialogue where narrator simultaneously claims to be and not be one of the twins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ identity slips, perspective confusions, or self-referential ambiguities that make a speaker both participant and external narrator; this particular inversion of standpoint yields comic bewilderment and amusement when handled with clarity of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic obsessional motifs (recurrence across contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain images or burdens recur persistently with shifting meanings (as in dreams or a song’s repeated burden), producing comic obsessional effects when transplanted across scenes or verses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately reuse a motif, phrase, or image across different contexts with small variations; the audience’s recognition plus shifting sense produces layered humor. Avoid mere repetition without transformation—comic value grows from changing implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as sympathetic relaxation and invitation to play
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience initially sympathises—adopts the character’s gestures and relaxes intellectual tension; comic absurdity invites the spectator to ‘join the game’, providing relief from the strain of thinking and ordinary social effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage comic moments that encourage the audience to momentarily suspend critical attention and participate imaginatively (play along). Use this to create rapport and relief; the comic’s relaxation is part of its appeal and should be timed to offer respite without cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter's social function: correction and repression of separatist tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions socially to repress separatist tendencies, convert rigidity into plasticity, re-adapt the individual to the whole, and to correct social impertinences (laughter can be a retort—'an even greater impertinence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing satirical or corrective comedy, frame laughter as a social corrective aimed at widely shared faults (e.g., vanity, professional arrogance). Recognize that laughter may be brusque rather than benevolent; its purpose can be to reshape sociability rather than merely to vindicate the laugher.
